title: Windowed Credit Gating and KV Hinting (prototype)
content:
Context and motivation:

We continue to see tenant-driven oscillations where noisy tenants briefly consume disproportionate slot/time budgets and cause tail latency spikes for co-tenants. Existing token-bucket-style approaches work for steady-state smoothing but struggle with: 
- short bursts that saturate KV/compute before bucket refill
- requests that would have benefitted from cached KV state but arrive as cold misses
- fairness across tenants when some clients send many short requests (chatty) and others send fewer long requests (batchy)

This prototype explores a lightweight admission layer that gates by a time-windowed credit pool (credit horizon) and augments admission decisions with KV-cache "hints" surfaced by request metadata. The goal: reduce tail latency and tail queue growth without rigid per-tenant hard caps that block good traffic or require extensive config.

High-level goals:
- Keep per-tenant CPU/GPU slot occupancy within a configurable horizon (time-window) rather than only instantaneous concurrency.
- Prioritize requests likely to hit KV cache or that are latency-sensitive (based on declared deadline or heuristics).
- Allow brief priority bursts for new or debug traffic but decay them quickly (grace window).
- Be incremental: a feature flagged, optionally enabled by customer, and observable via per-tenant metrics.

Terminology (informal):
- credit: an abstract unit representing a fraction of the horizon budget. Credits deplete on admission and replenish on a wall-clock window. Think of 1 credit ~= 100ms-worth-of-slot for a single GPU.
- horizon window: sliding wall-clock window (e.g., 10s) where we bound cumulative admitted slot-time per tenant.
- kv-hint: a lightweight tag attached to requests (client-provided or derived) indicating likely cache hit potential e.g. prefix hash, conversation-id, or explicit flag.
- soft-preempt token: a short-lived marker given to long-running requests that allows preemption/eviction preference when system is under pressure.

Design overview (core ideas):
1) Windowed credit pool per tenant
   - Each tenant has a fixed number of credits proportional to their SLA/commit (and scaled for free-tier). Credits refill continuously with a simple leaky-window model: refill_rate = max_credits / horizon_seconds.
   - On admission, we charge credit proportional to estimated slot-time: min(estimated, max_charge) where estimated is derived from model profile + request length (or a default). 
   - If tenant has insufficient credits, admission is rejected or put into a short backoff queue depending on priority.

2) Admission priority tiers
   - latency-sensitive (declared deadline / small prompt) -> allowed to borrow small overdraft credits (bounded) for short bursts with fast repayment.
   - cache-friendly (kv-hint positive) -> discounted charge (e.g., 50% cost) because KV-hits reduce runtime cost and improve tail latency.
   - background/low-priority -> charged full cost, may be delayed until credits replenish.

3) KV hinting integration
   - Clients may attach kv_hint metadata (e.g., conversation_id, prefix_hash). Runtime will map hint -> cache-score using a lightweight local predictor that tracks recent hit rates for hints and prefixes.
   - Cache-score is quantized into (high, medium, low) and mapped to a discount factor applied to charge.
   - If hint predictor is cold, do not discount until we observe hits; warm-up happens automatically.

4) Soft preemption and graceful eviction
   - When host-level pressure crosses threshold (e.g., queue depth, free slots), active requests can be marked as soft-preemptible if: they exceed expected duration or they belong to low-priority class.
   - Preemption is cooperative: the runtime signals the worker to checkpoint/stop; if worker cannot yield quickly, we favor not preempting latency-sensitive cached requests.

5) Short waiting Q and hedging policy
   - A tiny per-tenant fast-queue (N slots) for holding near-term requests that couldn't be admitted due to credits but may be cheap (cache-hit). These wait for up to wait_ms (e.g., 50-200ms) to see if KV predictor flips to hit. If still blocked, they are either rejected or downgraded to background.

Admission logic (pseudocode sketch):

  onRequest(req):
    tenant = req.tenant
    est_ms = estimate_slot_time(req)  // model profile + tokens, fallback 200ms
    base_charge = ceil(est_ms / CREDIT_UNIT_MS)
    hint_score = lookup_hint_predictor(req.kv_hint) // high/med/low/unknown
    discount = {high:0.5, med:0.8, low:1.0, unknown:1.0}[hint_score]
    effective_charge = max(1, floor(base_charge * discount))

    if tenant.credits >= effective_charge:
      admit(req), tenant.credits -= effective_charge
      attach_soft_preempt = (req.priority == background) and (est_ms > PREEMPT_THRESHOLD)
      if attach_soft_preempt: tag_request_soft_preempt(req)
    else:
      if req.priority == latency_sensitive and tenant.can_overdraft_small():
        admit_as_overdraft(req), tenant.record_overdraft(effective_charge)
      else if hint_score == high and req.priority != background:
        enqueue_in_fastwait(req) // allow brief wait for cache warm or slot to free
      else:
        reject_or_rate_limit(req)

Metrics to surface (per tenant + global):
- windowed_credit_total, credit_refill_rate, credit_usage_percent
- admitted_by_priority (latency/cache/background)
- kv_hint_hit_rate (per hint prefix bucket) and discount_applied_count
- overdraft_count and repayment_latency (how quickly overdrafts are recovered)
- fastwait enqueue/dequeue/reject counts and time distribution
- preempted_requests_count and success_of_preemption (did it release slot within grace?)

Why this is different from plain quotas or token-buckets:
- time-window semantics bound cumulative slot-time across bursts (not just instantaneous concurrency). That better maps to GPU cost and prevents short bursts from burning credit that should cover sustained load.
- KV hint discount creates an incentive alignment: cached requests are cheaper and should be prioritized since they improve throughput and reduce worker pressure.
- Fastwait queue is an optimistic micro-window for cheap cache-warm or short bursts: avoids rejecting requests that could be satisfied with tiny delay and high success probability.

Operational concerns and fallback modes:
- Mis-specified kv_hint from clients could be gamed; we'll only apply discounts after observed positive hit-rate for a given hint pattern. Start conservative: no discount until > X% observed hits in last M minutes.
- Overdrafts must be bounded and visible; use exponential backoff on future admissions if overdrafts spike.
- For Dedicated/Private customers who want strict SLAs, make the feature optional and configurable (horizon_seconds, credit_unit_ms, discounts, safe-mode where discount=1).

Experiment plan (small increments):
1) Shadow mode: compute effective_charge and log decisions, but do not enforce. Run for 2 weeks on a couple of clusters to collect signal.
2) Controlled beta: turn on admission enforcement for 10 low-risk tenants; expose metrics and an endpoint to refund credits in emergency.
3) Wide rollout with default conservative parameters (long horizon, small discounts) and automated rollback triggers (latency increase, error rate).

Implementation notes / rough data structures:
- tenant state: credits (float), last_refill_ts, overdraft_counter, fastwait_queue (bounded), hint_stats (LRU map of prefix -> {hits, lookups, last}). Keep hint_stats compact (count sketch or fixed-size LRU).
- credit arithmetic uses floats but stored as integer microcredits to avoid drift.
- evaluation: use production traces to simulate charging under proposed params and compute percentiles of rejected vs admitted across tenants.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- What is the right horizon length? 5-15s seems reasonable for slot-level accounting; shorter horizons penalize bursty but short-friendly workloads less.
- Should KV discount depend on expected token hit count (not just boolean)? More granular discounts mean better alignment but require more telemetry and complexity.
- How do we combine with global binpacking: credits may say admit but the host has no slots; need a two-stage check (global admission then host assignment).
- How to surface transparent billing implications when discounting changes apparent unit-cost for tenant usage? Potentially confusing for customers.

Notes-to-self / TODO:
- Build a simulator to replay last 30 days of traffic and compute delta in tail-95/99 latency when applying discount vs not. (Liam volunteering)
- Add a TTLed LRU for hint predictors and experiment with threshold for enabling discounts (Sana to prototype).
- Draft UX for tenant settings: horizon, credit_unit_ms, discount-enable, fastwait_ms.
- Add a safety kill-switch on the control plane to zero discounts and immediately refund overdrafts if needed.

Appendix: small worked example
- tenant A: horizon=10s, credit_unit=100ms -> max_credits=100 (10s/100ms)
- tenant sends 40 requests each estimated 200ms in 3s: base_charge=2 each => 80 credits used quickly, leaving 20 credits for next 7s. If many more arrive, they'll be backpressured even if instantaneous concurrency is low.
- if kv_hint predicts high for some of those requests, discount 50% -> effective_charge=1 -> they consume only 40 credits, smoothing the window.

This feels like a pragmatic middle ground between rigid per-tenant concurrency caps and fully dynamic admission that only looks at instantaneous resource usage. It should reduce short-term congestion and prioritize requests that are cheaper to serve (cache hits) without forcing customers into complex tuning.

Feedback welcome — especially on heuristics for hint scoring and conservative thresholds for enabling discounting in production.

— Marco
